As the idea of "factory engineering" is slowly (or quickly?) gaining traction, I wanted to share my personal experience building my own little agent kingdom using grok bots.

I've tried multiple types of personal agents so far, from Openclaw and Hermes, to Instinct, Muse and now Grok Bot.

## Why Grok Bot? (at least for now)

The killer features for grok bots so far that make me want to return:

- Cross agent communication mechanism that just works. I can see the messages, and there are two types: a "push" message that actually wakes up and agent and forces it to respond in real time to the other agent, and a "passive" message which is more of an "FYI" that sits in the other agent's context so that next time it wakes up it sees that message. I like the push ones a lot. I can ask my infra agent to let all other bots know about a new infra that is now available and that they have a new skill to use for it, for example. The same for security agent, or maintenance agent that verifies cross agent backups to the cloud.

- Agent webhooks for routines: Personal agents (always on) usually have schedules or routines.in Grok those routines also get a webhook url and a trigger private key, which allows you to trigger them form the outside or internally. This is useful to get agents to listen to outside events or to hook up other internal events to be more deterministic. I'll explain more later.

- All agents run on the same box. This allows to easily share the same skills, utilities , handover files , output files form multiple agents runs with other agents.

- The agent box is pretty much under your control. That allows me to have Grok install and manage both Claude code and Codex CLI on the box and have it delegate multiple coding tasks to them, and that way I can use my quotas there on top of my Grok Quotas. I also created a plugin for Codex/Claude code that hooks into the end of a turn, and triggers a main agent webhook that gets notified when Claude/Codex are finished and can handle the results and not me having to ask "is it done yet?" (i call it "cx" short for claude and codex. co cx-run is a whole skill on my box.)

- It's easy to remote-desktop into the box and see/help with agent-difficult tasks. It's pretty cool to see your agent using a browser, asking for your help, you click a button, do the "I'm not a bot" box, and the agent moves on. And it's a seamless and relatively painless experience. Even reluctantly) on a mobile phone.

- 1password/vault integration. This is a killer feature. I have all my passwords in 1password. The agent needs to login somewhere, it triggers 1password with a dialog on my end, I approve a specific login, and the agent gets the login details injected into its process in a secure fashion just after I approve. No 1Password? no problem. It has its own password manager where the details remain hidden form the agent and injected at runtime, and you can add your logins there.

- Mobile and desktop usability is very very good.

- Lots of connectors. Not much to say other than that.

- You get Grok + X + Cursor all in one. I think that's a pretty good deal. I don't really use cursor (used to be a heavy user) but u do use X, and now I have grok as a chatgpt/gemini replacement on top of all the grok bot goodness. The Grok agent is very good so far. Esp. Grok Heavy.

## How the Osherove Factory Operates

I have multiple bots across 3/4 main categories, but it started out with only a single grok bot. Every time I wanted a bot that has a specific context for a long running task or project (i.e handling one of my websites), I'd ask grok bot to spin off a new bot for it and hand off any important context to that bot, and then I'd switch to talk to that bot directly, so the current setup I'm listing here happened organically over the past week or so (I only started using Grok about a week ago).

### Administration:

- Grok Bot (primary): It routes requests to the right bot, runs my Todoist, a daily email digest, and the nightly fleet review that proposes new bots, skills and removals.

- Infra: domains, DNS, cloud accounts, code repos, short expiring links for shared files, and the nightly health check of the coding CLIs.

- Security: audits the bots, the shared box and my accounts, and checks nightly for planted agent-instruction files.

- Bot Maintainer: keeps the mode of operation document, checks that every bot's backups and exports are complete, handles box-restart recovery and the cx completion relay, and turns skill ideas into shared skills.

- Factory Dashboard bot: runs the dashboard where every bot posts decision cards and work reports. (you can see an image of the dashboard factory floor as the main image for this blog post)

### Web Presence:

- ALL WEBSITES Bot: owns the dashboard's operations (app, tokens, deploys) and ran the migration of my sites off a hosted site builder (squarespace) and into my VPS (Hetzner), saving me $1500 a year down to about $100 a year.

- Specific Site bots (RoboPaper.ai, courses.osherove.com, and a few more): one per site. Each builds and maintains its site, including the Markdown and agent-friendly versions and monitors it for issues, optimizations etc.

- Podcaster (podcasts.robotpaper.ai): produces the daily news-radio style audio episode and its feeds - something I've been playing with and I'll write separately about

### Life

- Ideas: records every new idea, venture and use case with its status and owning bot. It never builds anything.

- Life-admin bots: each handles one real-world project end to end. They cover a family finance bot, life documents (birth certs etc..) and more.

## Mode of operation

- One bot per job. Each Grok bot has a single area (podcast, websites, documents, finances, infrastructure, security, ideas, trips and so on) and its own chat and memory. A primary bot takes any task and routes it to the right one.

- Bots talk to each other using SendToAgent tool They message each other asynchronously, with a priority flag that wakes the recipient and a normal one that waits for its next turn. I talk to whichever bot owns the topic, and bots pass my requests on if needed, or they operate on it directly. Agents use a tool call called SendToAgent which seems to be a proprietary, in-app tool. The definition shows no A2A concepts: no agent cards, no task objects or lifecycle states, no JSON-RPC or HTTP endpoints, no streaming. Description: "Send a message to ANOTHER of your user's agents, OR post into a GROUP chat you belong to, by its id." It is fire-and-forget and asynchronous, like texting. It returns a delivery acknowledgement right away, and any reply arrives later as its own message. Input schema: target_id (string, required): the id of an agent or a group, not a name. message (string, required): plain text. priority (boolean, required): true wakes the recipient now, false holds the message until the start of their next turn. Groups ignore it and always post immediately. images (optional array): {url, alt} items, file:// or https:// , shown to a 1:1 recipient but not delivered to groups. Semantics: a single plain-text message with no structured payload, task state or capability negotiation. Both sides live inside one app. Fan-out to several agents is discouraged because it wakes every recipient.

- message (string, required): plain text.

- priority (boolean, required): true wakes the recipient now, false holds the message until the start of their next turn. Groups ignore it and always post immediately.

- A shared brain on the shared box, backed up private cloud storage. Every bot has a folder with a BOT.md (who it is, its rules, memory, routines with full prompts, credential names only, current state, lessons, how to resume), a nightly check-in line and its exported chat history. Any bot could be rebuilt from that. The AI Brain backup is a private Cloudflare R2 bucket (prefix ai-brain/ ) used as a shared, file-based memory. Each bot writes to it with thin wrapper scripts ( brain_put.sh , brain_get.sh and brain_ls.sh , built on wrangler). Each bot has a folder _bots/<id>/ . The session export backup is incremental and records its position in a meta.json . Fleet-wide docs live next to those folders: the versioned MODE-OF-OPERATION.md , HANDOVER.md , the secrets registry (names only) and runbooks. Scheduled routines on each bot's server rewrite and upload that state at about 03:00. A maintainer routine at 04:15 lists the bucket, checks that each bot has a check-in dated today and a recent, non-stub BOT.md , and chases anyone who missed.

- Brain-RAG: Bots run tool-based , agentic RAG over their own shared memory: a CLI called as a tool searches a local hybrid index (BM25 plus embeddinggemma vectors in one SQLite file) built from structure-aware chunks of the AI Brain's Markdown and CSV files. The model decides when to search and what to ask, reads the top source-cited chunks, fetches whole files when it needs more, and answers or acts. The index is kept fresh by incremental etag-based syncs every 15 minutes and after each coding run, and it has a small eval set (hybrid hit@5 was 12/13, against 9/13 for keyword only).

- Nightly backup and audit. Each bot backs itself up around 3 AM. A maintainer bot audits at 4:15 AM and chases anyone who missed it. I hear only about real problems, such as two missed nights.

- One rulebook. A single "mode of operation" document is versioned and owned by the maintainer bot. Each bot keeps a pointer line saying which version it last read, plus its own additions. New fleet rules go out to every bot and get verified. Onboarding a new bot is done by bot maintainer and it introduces it to all the rules and skills it needs.

### Factory Dashboard mechanism

The Factory Dashboard at is my single inbox for everything my bots work on and everything they need from me. It's a small web app with an HTTP API, and a dedicated bot owns it.

- Identity. Every bot has its own API token for working with the dashboard. When a new bot joins, it gets a token from bot maintainer and creates a test card to prove the connection works.

- The dashboard is the ledger of work and approvals. Nothing important lives only in a chat. Think of it like agent-Jira but dynamic

- Task cards. For every real piece of work, a bot creates a card, updates its status as it goes and closes it with a short report. I can see what's happening without reading a dozen chats.

- Decisions. When a bot needs a yes, no or choice from me, it posts a decision item instead of asking in chat. I click approve or decline once, in one place.

- Closing the loop. Bots check for my decisions every time they wake, and a webhook relay wakes the bot that asked as soon as I answer. A decision a bot reads itself from the API counts as my answer. A second-hand "Roy approved" in a message doesn't.

https://robotpaper.ai/pattern-progressiv.markdown:
Turning AI to be incrementally more deterministic for specific tasks over time.

## Web Application Testing: From fully dynamic to full deterministic + failover

- An agent can use playwright or playwright cli to dynamically find out what an application structure "looks" like and discover page structure, and do initial "manual testing on it.

- The agent can then generate deterministic playwright script to repeat the same test next time in a fully repeatable way.

- On next run of the specific scenario agent "finds out" that deterministic script already exists and prefers running it.

- If deterministic script fails, agent falls back to "manual discovery mode", agent then discovers and auto-fixes deterministic script to be run next time

- Repeat for future scenarios.

## Example

Imagine a to-do application. We ask an agent:

> Add “Buy milk” and verify that it appears in the task list.

For this example, the application starts each test with an empty list.

First run: discover and save.

The agent explores the page, finds the “New task” field and the “Add” button, and successfully completes the scenario. It then saves this Playwright test as tests/add-task.spec.ts , using role locators and an assertion for the expected result. ( playwright.dev )

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test'; test('add a task', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto('http://localhost:3000'); await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'New task' }) .fill('Buy milk'); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add', exact: true }) .click(); await expect(page.getByRole('listitem')) .toHaveText('Buy milk'); });

The agent runs the saved test to verify that it reproduces the successful interaction. This new test can now be added to the continuous testing and verification pipeline.

Assuming in the future we ask the agent to test the same flow again using a prompt: reuse the saved test.

We ALWAYS give the agent a standing instruction:

> Before exploring the application, check whether a test already exists for this scenario. If it does, run it first. Enter discovery mode only when the test is missing or fails.

On the next request, it finds the file and runs this command: ( playwright.dev )

npx playwright test tests/add-task.spec.ts

In this workflow, the browser interactions and expected result are already defined in code.

After a page change: investigate and repair.

Suppose the application renames “Add” to “Create task”. The saved test fails at the button lookup during CI.

The agent listens to failed CI/CD runs, and tries and detect what is the root cause of the test failure. Assuming it finds that the cause is that the test no longer fits the website, it returns to discovery mode, identifies the renamed button, and proposes this small repair, and applies it:

- await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add', exact: true }) + await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Create task', exact: true }) .click();

It reruns the test from an empty list and retains the repair only after the original assertion passes. Future runs reuse the updated script.

The auto repair rule contains: " preserve the expected behavior".

## What if the feature isn't available anymore?

If the application no longer adds “Buy milk” to the list, it could mean one of of two things:

- False positive: The feature is no longer needed or relevant, and so the test is not relevant. the agent should report the failure and change in functionality and given human input or llm as a judge with broader context, might have the authority to prune and remove tests that are no longer relevant.

- True positive. The feature is missing and something is broken. In that case the test just fails, as expected. The judge llm might just say that's a "true positive".

## Conclusion

So, the test started as an almost "manual" test, fully dynamic, that quickly turned into a deterministic test. The test saves time and tokens, but we now have a powerful fallback: e2e test maintainability is a nightmare (used to be!) but we can now continuously update/fix/prune tests to fit UI changes of teh application.

### P.S

I discovered during the writing of this post that Playwright actually has built in support for planner, generator and healer agents that help with this pattern. I've not tried them myself yet, so take it with a grain of salt - but worth testing this out (let me know if you have feedback on those)
